summary: The video presents a practical Photoshop-based workflow for landscape tonal development that centers on creating a directional light feel, shading toward that light, and building depth through dodge/burn and edge contrasts. The presenter contrasts traditional dodge/burn with 'clone painting' (clone-stamp) as alternative methods, then demonstrates sky-horizon fusion to remove harsh horizons and enhance depth. A strong emphasis on tonal processing (especially black-and-white first) precedes recoloring via split-toning and selective color. The speaker also covers RAW-based dynamic-range expansion, luminosity adjustments, diffusion and glow, and cautions about monitor versus print results, urging hands-on painting as the core artistic skill beneath any tool-based workflow.

sections.title: Establishing a directional light and shading toward it
sections.description: The speaker demonstrates creating a directional light source and shading the image toward that light to create depth and a sense of three-dimensional form. The emphasis is on controlling light across the scene to guide the viewer’s eye.

sections.title: Dodge and burn as painterly tonal control
sections.description: The presenter frames shading as a painterly act, using dodge and burn to sculpt light and texture and stressing its centrality to both black-and-white and color processing.

sections.title: Long-lens considerations and painting as a core workflow
sections.description: A compact discussion ties the approach to long-lens landscapes, noting light, atmosphere, and angular light are essential, with shading and brushwork serving as the primary control mechanism.

sections.title: Black-and-white as learning ground; color workflow intro
sections.description: The speaker argues for mastering tonal processing in black and white before color and introduces three color-shot models (partially colored, fully colored, recolored) and the concept of split-toning as a tonal-to-color bridge.

sections.title: Color workflow strategies and tool choice
sections.description: The workflow is articulated: build tonal structure first, then add color; the speaker demonstrates choosing tools (dodging/burning vs clone painting) and explains why separating tonal work from color work can simplify processing.

sections.title: Building depth via near-to-far transitions and subject separation
sections.description: The speaker demonstrates creating tonal transitions that pull the eye toward the main subject (the tree) by enhancing foreground shadows and sky contrast, plus selective darkening/lightening to separate subjects from the background.

sections.title: Sky-to-horizon fusion to remove harsh horizons
sections.description: A practical sky cloning technique is shown to blend the sky with the landscape horizon, eliminating harsh lines and creating a more seamless, depth-enhancing transition between sky and land.

sections.title: RAW-based tonal expansion and color reintroduction
sections.description: The speaker discusses expanding dynamic range in RAW, then reintroducing color via color balance and selective color, emphasizing the order of operations: tonal work first, then color.

sections.title: Diffusion, luminosity and glow; monitor vs print caveat
sections.description: A key caution about diffusion-based edits and their print fidelity is discussed. The presenter explains how diffusion can create glow when paired with luminosity adjustments and stresses testing across screens and in print.
